title: Pacific Christianity
hookLine: from Fiji to Samoa, village churches fill with harmony on Sunday

lines: SUNDAY, A VILLAGE, THE SHOPS SHUT.
cards: Sunday morning, a village on a Pacific island. The shops are shut. The road is quiet.

Then, from a white church near the water, the singing starts. No organ, no screen with the words. Just voices, men low, women high, parts weaving over and under each other, so full the windows seem to hum.
A visitor stands outside and doesn't want to go in, in case it stops. In Samoa, in Tonga, in Fiji, Sunday has a sound.

teach.b: The gospel came to the Pacific by ship, with missionaries from Britain and elsewhere. That story has its hard chapters, as mission stories often do, tangled with trade and empire. But it didn't stay a foreign thing.
Islanders themselves became the teachers and pastors, and some sailed on to other islands, carrying the faith in their own languages. Some island readers find their place already named in the Psalms.

teach.h: LET THE MULTITUDE OF ISLES BE GLAD.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof."
Isaiah says it too: "Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof."
Hymns arrived with the missionaries, and island singers took them somewhere new, folding in their own ways of singing in many parts at once. A Tongan or Samoan choir doesn't just perform a hymn.

teach.h: A CHOIR BUILDS A HYMN, VOICE BY VOICE.
teach.b: It builds one, voice by voice. That's the quiet lesson inside harmony. In unison, everyone sings the same note.
In harmony, everyone sings a different note, and the notes fit. No one voice carries the song alone; if the basses drop out, everyone hears the hole.
The letter to the Colossians tells an early church to be "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." One another.
Singing, in that letter, is something a church does together, not something it watches.

how: In Pacific island churches, Sunday worship is often marked by full congregational and choir singing in several parts, frequently without instruments, and in some island villages Sunday itself is kept as a day of rest.

o: a church founded on one island that rules all the others
the islands' faith, carried by islanders and sung in many parts
a faith kept only by foreign missionaries on the islands

games.q: the island choirs — tap the pairs.
p: let them be glad, says the psalm
in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs

s: "let the multitude of isles be glad thereof."
Christianity spread across the Pacific only through European missionaries
islanders became teachers and pastors and carried it on to other islands themselves.
in harmony, everyone sings the same note
that's unison. in harmony each voice sings a different note, and the notes fit.

games.q: you're in the bass line of an island choir and you lose your place. the others are still singing. what happens?
o: nobody notices; the melody carries it.
everyone hears the hole where the low part was.
the choir stops and starts over.
games.why: in harmony no one voice carries the song alone, so a missing part is heard by all. Paul pictures a church singing to one another.

practice: Hum the first line of a hymn, or any song that has carried you somewhere, low in your chest.
Hum it again and listen to the room around you, the fridge, traffic, a bird, and notice how your note sits among them, one part of a larger sound.
If you pray, let the humming be your prayer, or say the psalm's line, let the multitude of isles be glad; if not, simply keep humming, and listen.
